title: Encoding a structure: a work item
summary: A work item encodes as its fields in a fixed order: fixed-width numbers in $\mathcal{E}_4$, $\mathcal{E}_8$ and $\mathcal{E}_2$, hashes as themselves, and the variable-length parts (the payload, the imports, the extrinsics) each preceded by their length. This vector's item encodes to 236 octets.

rows.label: Payload $\mathbf{y}$, with its length
cells: $\updownarrow$ (C.8): $\mathcal{E}$ of the length, then the octets

rows.label: Import 1
cells: the root as itself, then $\mathcal{E}_2$ of the index

rows.label: Import 2
cells: the root as itself, then $\mathcal{E}_2$ of the index

rows.label: Import 3
cells: the root as itself, then $\mathcal{E}_2$ of the index

rows.label: Extrinsic 1
cells: the hash as itself, then $\mathcal{E}_4$ of the length

rows.label: Extrinsic 2
cells: the hash as itself, then $\mathcal{E}_4$ of the length

params: no chain parameters: the codec alone
notes: Long runs show their first four octets and their last few: an import ends with its index in $\mathcal{E}_2$, an extrinsic with its length in $\mathcal{E}_4$.
Every count and length here is below 128, so $\mathcal{E}$ writes each as one octet (eq. C.6).
name: codec-work-item
check: The pieces above, joined in order, are the model's encoding, and it equals the vector's `work_item.bin` octet for octet. The model's decoder also reads the `.bin` back to a term that encodes to the same octets. `lake build codectest` makes both comparisons on every codec vector.
